summary: In this episode, Fathers Andrew Stephen Damick and Stephen De Young explore the non-canonical Acts of the Apostles, focusing on the Acts of Paul, Acts of Peter, Acts of John, and Acts of Thomas. They discuss the historical context, the traditions preserved in these texts, and their significance for understanding the early Church. The hosts emphasize that these texts are not the source of traditions but witnesses to them, and they address the question of Gnostic influence, showing that while some texts contain ambiguous or Gnostic elements, others are explicitly anti-Gnostic. The episode also covers the role of these texts in the Seventh Ecumenical Council and the importance of reading them with discernment, as part of the broader Orthodox tradition.

entities.title: Acts of Paul
entities.summary: A second-century text containing traditions about St. Paul, including the Acts of Paul and Thecla, correspondence with Corinth, and the martyrdom of Paul. It is considered historically reliable in parts and was even read as canonical in some churches.

entities.title: Acts of Peter
entities.summary: A late second-century text collecting traditions about St. Peter in Rome, including his conflict with Simon Magus and his crucifixion upside down. It is anti-Gnostic and contains the famous 'Quo Vadis' episode.

entities.title: Acts of John
entities.summary: A mid-second-century text with traditions about St. John, including raising the dead and his peaceful death. It contains a later Gnostic insertion, which was used by the Manichaeans and was debated at the Seventh Ecumenical Council.

entities.title: Acts of Thomas
entities.summary: A text about St. Thomas's mission to India, including his being sold as a slave, building a palace in heaven, and performing exorcisms. It is ambiguous regarding Gnosticism and contains the Hymn of the Pearl.

entities.title: St. Thecla
entities.summary: A disciple of St. Paul, known for her virginity and preaching. She is a major figure in the Acts of Paul and is venerated as a proto-martyr, especially in the Antiochian Church.

entities.title: Simon Magus
entities.summary: A sorcerer who appears in the canonical Acts and in the Acts of Peter as a representative of Gnosticism. He attempts to buy the Holy Spirit and later performs magical feats in Rome, ultimately defeated by St. Peter.

entities.title: St. Nikephoros of Constantinople
entities.summary: A ninth-century Patriarch of Constantinople who compiled a list of apocryphal texts that are beneficial for private reading. His list is used as a guide for which apocrypha are acceptable.

concepts.title: Apocryphal Acts of the Apostles
concepts.summary: Non-canonical texts that narrate the deeds and traditions of the apostles after the events of the Book of Acts. They are considered valuable for private reading and contain early traditions, but are not read publicly in church.

concepts.title: Gnosticism
concepts.summary: A heretical movement in early Christianity that taught the material world is evil and created by a lesser god, and that salvation comes through secret knowledge. The hosts discuss how some apocryphal acts are anti-Gnostic, while others contain ambiguous elements.

concepts.title: Tradition vs. Text
concepts.summary: The idea that traditions about the apostles existed before and independently of the written texts. The texts are witnesses to these traditions, not their origin. This is crucial for understanding the reliability of the apocryphal acts.

concepts.title: Canon and Authority
concepts.summary: The authority of a text is determined by the Church's use of it in public worship, not by its content alone. The hosts discuss how canonicity is an objective fact of church practice, and how apocrypha are categorized for private reading.

claims.text: The Acts of Paul contains elements that are broadly historically reliable, even according to secular scholars, and was considered canonical by some churches in the early centuries.
The apocryphal acts are not the source of traditions about the apostles but are witnesses to pre-existing traditions, similar to the Gospels.
The Christian embrace of voluntary virginity, as exemplified by St. Thecla, is the origin of the concept of sexual consent in Western culture.
The Acts of Peter is clearly anti-Gnostic, using Simon Magus as a representative of Gnosticism and showing his defeat by St. Peter.
The Acts of John contains a later Gnostic insertion (chapters 87-105) that is identifiable by differences in style, vocabulary, and theology, and was used by the Manichaeans.
The Acts of Thomas is ambiguous regarding Gnosticism; it can be read either in a Gnostic or an Orthodox way, making it suitable for private reading with discernment.

scriptural_links.summary: Christ's command to be witnesses in Judea, Samaria, and to the ends of the earth is the geographic through-line of the Book of Acts, and the apocryphal acts show the fulfillment of this command.
St. Luke's reference to his first book (the Gospel) as covering what Christ began to do and teach is used to explain that Acts is the continuation of Christ's work through the Church.
The idea that not everything Jesus did is recorded is applied to the apostles, justifying the existence of traditions not in the New Testament.
The Tree of Life is connected to the Cross and the Eucharist, as the Cross is seen as the restoration of the Tree of Life, and the leaves of the tree heal the nations.
Balaam's donkey speaking is referenced in the Acts of Thomas, where a talking donkey claims descent from Balaam's ass, showing the text's use of Old Testament imagery.

glossary.definition: Texts that are not read publicly in church but are considered beneficial for private reading. The term means 'hidden' or 'private'.
Relating to Gnosticism, a heretical belief system that the material world is evil and salvation comes through secret knowledge.
The movement against the veneration of icons, which was condemned at the Seventh Ecumenical Council. The Acts of John was used by iconoclasts in their arguments.
A major Gnostic religion founded by Mani, which used a version of the Acts of John with a Gnostic insertion.
